--- 

Our goal today is to _review_ everything we have discussed to date about
regression. After a brief run of the conceptual issues listed above, I'll
open the floor for questions and then start working through some examples. 
Let's start with a relatively simple data set: 

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
births <- read_csv("https://michael-weylandt.com/STAT3106/data/births.csv")
```

```{r}
#| message: false
births <- read_csv("data/births.csv")
```

This is a relatively simple data set, where the variable of interest is
the number of children born (or at least reported to the SSA) in the US
every day from the beginning of `r min(births$year)` to the end of
`r max(births$year)`, for a total of `r NROW(births)` days. To make the
analysis a bit easier, I have separated year, month, day into variables, 
as well as setting up different "day of week" and "day of year" variables.

```{r}
skimr::skim(births)
```

Before we get to modeling, let's do some visual EDA: 

```{r}
births |> 
    mutate(date = make_date(year, month, day)) |> 
    ggplot(aes(x=date, y=births)) + 
    geom_line() + 
    scale_x_date() + 
    xlab("Date") + 
    ylab("Number of Reported Births") + 
    theme_bw()
```

We immediately see that the time (date) effect isn't _linear_ but there is
nevertheless an upwards trend that a linear model might capture: 

```{r}
births |> 
    mutate(date = make_date(year, month, day)) |> 
    ggplot(aes(x=date, y=births)) + 
    geom_line() + 
    scale_x_date() + 
    xlab("Date") + 
    ylab("Number of Reported Births") + 
    theme_bw() + 
    stat_smooth(method="lm", 
                se=FALSE)
```

Not great, but about as good as we might expect. If we use `ggplot2`'s 
default `gam` smoother, we definitely see a better fit. 

```{r}
births |> 
    mutate(date = make_date(year, month, day)) |> 
    ggplot(aes(x=date, y=births)) + 
    geom_line() + 
    scale_x_date() + 
    xlab("Date") + 
    ylab("Number of Reported Births") + 
    theme_bw() + 
    stat_smooth(se=FALSE)
```

We see here the end of the baby boom, a small decrease, and then a smoother
rise as the US population grew (more people, more parents, more babies). 

The regular 'jagged' patterns to this data suggest we might want to look
at a day of year effect and a day of week effect: 

```{r}
births |> 
    mutate(date = make_date(year, month, day), 
           wday = wday(date, label=TRUE)) |> 
    group_by(wday) |> 
    summarize(births = mean(births)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x=wday, y=births)) + 
    geom_col() + 
    theme_bw() + 
    xlab("Day of Week") + 
    ylab("Average Number of Births")
```

Similarly, 

```{r}
births |> 
    mutate(date = make_date(year, month, day), 
           month_name = month(date, label=TRUE)) |> 
    group_by(month_name) |> 
    summarize(births = mean(births)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x=month_name, y=births)) + 
    geom_col() + 
    theme_bw() + 
    xlab("Month") + 
    ylab("Average Number of Births")
```

If we plot by day of year, we see a hint of some holiday effects:

```{r}
births |> 
    group_by(day_of_year) |> 
    summarize(births = mean(births)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x=day_of_year, y=births)) + 
    geom_line() + 
    theme_bw() + 
    xlab("Day of Year") + 
    ylab("Average Number of Births")
```

Though day of year will not be a perfect proxy due to certain moving 
holidays and leap year effects. 

That's pretty much all the structure we can get from this data set, so let's
start modeling it. As seen above, we see several _non-linear_ effects, so
let's break out our non-linear toolkit, _additive models_ from `mgcv`. 

```{r}
#| message: false
library(mgcv)
library(broom)
gam(births ~ year, data=births)
```

By default, a GAM is just a linear model, so we get the simple fit we 
saw before: 

```{r}
gam(births ~ year, data=births) |> 
    broom::augment(newdata=births) |> 
    mutate(date=make_date(year, month, day)) |> 
    ggplot(aes(x=date)) + 
    geom_line(aes(y=births), color="black") + 
    geom_line(aes(y=.fitted), color="red4")
```

(Test yourself: why is this 'step pattern' an artifact? How might we 
avoid it?)
